content:
This year was my first time really building out a growth team.

One of my favorite parts about growth is getting to use both the creative and analytical parts of your brain. One week we're building out our TAM and internal tools; the next we're testing a new acquisition channel, shipping a free tool, or rebuilding part of our GTM system.

The work changes constantly, which has made me think a lot more about the traits that carry across different problems. It's also probably why none of the people we've brought on have particularly conventional backgrounds.

Rocco Totaro grew up in a village of ~7,000 people in Italy where somehow close to half the people are also named Rocco. He started the first Italian frat at Bocconi, studied data science, and is one of the most relentlessly curious people I've met.

During his interview, I gave him a timed case study around building an actual system. The problem was intentionally ambiguous. I wanted to see what he built, but also how he thought about the architecture, the trade-offs he made, what would break at scale, and what he'd do differently with more time.

He crushed it and went well beyond the ask. Before his first day, he was already texting me asking for things he could start working on.

A lot of how we work together now is still some version of me saying "figure it out" and him coming back with something better than I had in mind.

Alexandra Starr came from growth equity, but what stood out to me was everything she had built outside of work. She started a dropshipping business in high school that grew to 100k+ followers, and later a women's poker community with hundreds of members.

Throughout the interview process, it was clear that she just got people. She had great judgment, cared a lot about connecting people, and thought about community like an actual human. Now she's building out our events and community strategy.

Jenifer joined us last week as a GTM engineering intern. She’s studying Systems Design Engineering at the University of Waterloo, and we found her because she cold DMed our CTO.

For her interview project, she built a deliverability domain checker across ~30 sources, turned it into something that could actually be useful, and explained the system behind it really well. In her first week, she helped ship our new use case library with 75 workflows.

Those are the traits I care about most when hiring: agency, curiosity, drive, judgment, and evidence that someone builds things.

Very lucky to work with Rocco, Alex, and Jenifer.

content:
On Wednesday, I walked through how we’ve been rebuilding outbound at Unify at Knock’s Marketing Engineer Meetup in SF.

Our product has changed, and so has how we think about targeting, rep workflows, and what we build as a growth team.

A few things we got into:
- Combining automated outbound and rep outreach around what was working for reps. Same peak meeting volume, a higher qualification rate, and reps going from missing quota to far exceeding it.

- Rebuilding our TAM around the pain points our new product solves best. We combine account fit with signals like hiring, tech stack, and renewal windows to help reps decide where to focus and why now. Reps can inspect the scoring and sort by fit, timing, or individual data points.

- Finding useful context in calls, replies, and the CRM. A prospect mentions a contract renewal; the rep gets it in Slack with the original quote and source at the right time. A customer asks for a feature; we can find them again when it ships.

- Reusing that data to plan events (a US heat map of where prospects and companies are), run smaller targeted campaigns, and build personalized ABM pages reps can use in outreach.

With a growth team of 3, we start with the ideal outcome and work backward. We aim to ship a useful first version in a day or two, improve it through use, and carry the research and tools into the next project.

Learned a lot from Scott Strand, Bryanna Clancy, Darshil Gandhi, and Ian McClanan. 

Thanks to Knock for organizing, and Beth Saunders and the Amplitude x Statsig team for hosting!

content:
When I joined Unify, I was handed one challenge: double the pipeline from automated outbound. I'd be using Unify to grow Unify, so whether it worked would shape how much the team believed in what we were selling.

I already knew the tool. I'd onboarded it at my previous two companies, and I joined because I believed in the product and the team. But belief doesn't move a number. It started hard. The systems were struggling, and every play looked exhausted. I had to strip down every workflow and build more creative ways to do outreach at scale. Three months of going deep on almost nothing else, and we nearly tripled the monthly output.

That stretch changed how I think about growth. The alpha for the fastest-growing startups has shifted to distribution: unique data and systems that generate pipeline. My job, at a high level, is building those systems, mostly through automation, running new experiments every week.

One thing didn't sit right, though. We ran "outbound" and "automated outbound" as two separate channels, borrowing each other's best practices but goaled and operated apart. Earlier this year, we stopped. We aligned the incentives and rebuilt the architecture so the two were one motion (more on that in a future post). 

Our best outbound reps, it turned out, already work like a growth team:
1. They chase the highest-leverage opportunities, ten high-intent leads over a hundred cold ones.
2. They double down on what's working the moment they see it, a channel, a message, an angle.
3. They adapt constantly and will do whatever it takes to hit the number.

Put those reps and those systems on the same motion, and the old line between human judgment and machine scale stops mattering.

Today, we're launching a new Unify, purpose-built for reps. What used to live across five tools, a list-builder, an enrichment vendor, a sequencer, a data pull, a deliverability tool, now happens in one chat. A rep describes who they want to reach and why, and Unify builds the list, finds the contacts, writes the sequence, and handles the sending. 

Idea to execution in minutes, in one place.

We just had our best weeks ever for qualified pipeline 🙂 

Austin Hughes Connor Heggie 🚀

content:
Had a great time speaking at Gumloop's "How Top Marketers Are Using Agents" event last Thursday, in a room filled with 150+ GTM leaders and founders.

I demoed the new Unify and talked about:
1) Our shift to a self-serve product (chat interface with 40+ data sources)
2) How we think about automation vs manual touches internally
3) The importance of rapid experimentation/focus

Talking with the other speakers and attendees, the thing that stuck was that the constraint in growth isn't ideas, but rather throughput. There are more tools to try, more playbooks to copy, and more strategies to test than any team can get through in a day. Anyone in startup land knows the feeling of always being behind, putting out fires, and playing catch-up.

Speed of learning is what matters: how fast you can get to a signal and whether you're building things that compound instead of rebuilding the same overhead every month. Agents are doing all the grunt work now, but across every demo, human judgment and thinking were intentionally kept in the loop.

Thanks to Joseph Bath and Dima Khlopkov for having me. If anyone wants free Unify credits to try the new product, please comment below or DM me :)
